newsitem.title: USA: U.S. budget blueprint to get airing in committees.
newsitem.headline: U.S. budget blueprint to get airing in committees.

text.p: White House and congressional negotiators worked Wednesday to tie up loose ends on a joint framework to balance the federal budget, moving it to the next key step on the road to enactment.
The House and Senate budget committees planned to give a full airing Thursday to the budget resolution, which outlines spending and tax plans needed to balance the budget by 2002.

The federal budget was last balanced in 1969. The Congressional Budget Office has said it expects the budget deficit to be $67 billion in fiscal 1997, down from nearly $300 billion in the early 1990s.

Until now, the budget deal had been in the hands of a few key negotiators representing President Clinton and congressional leaders, who held frequent and long meetings in a basement hideaway office of the U.S. Capitol.
The committee consideration of the plan will offer a wider opinion of the delicately-carved agreement.
The White House and congressional leaders announced with much hoopla and flag-waving May 2 that they had reached an historic accord to balance the budget over five years.
Since that announcement, Democrats and Republicans have disagreed about what was actually contained in the budget deal, which they termed "a verbal handshake" because nothing was written down.
Now, the budget plan will be accompanied by a 40-page outline of priorities agreed upon by the White House and Republican leaders.
"We have the votes to get it out of the budget committee, but we want to get it in a bipartisan way," Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, said.

If the budget resolution makes it through the committee as expected, it would go before the full Senate early next week, Lott said. House Republican leaders said they hoped it would pass by May 23, when Congress takes a one-week recess.
In another example of how the two sides have differed in their interpretations of the budget agreement, Lott and a White House official gave conflicting versions of one issue.

White House Legislative Director John Hilley said agreement had been reached to have separate votes on spending and tax legislation by having two so-called "reconciliation" bills that enact the details of a budget.
Lott said a short time later it was unclear whether the Senate would be able to take up tax and spending legislation separately because of a Senate rule.

Lott and House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, were also drafting a letter to Clinton on the tax agreements. The budget deal calls for $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years, and those parameters were expected to remain.

One tax provision that had heads spinning was a proposed $35 billion in education tax credits for higher education, which had been a Clinton priority. The White House believed there was an agreement to include that amount in the budget, while the chairman of the House tax-writing committee cast doubt on it.
Lott said the tax letter would state that up to $35 billion in the first five years would be considered in the budget for the education tax credits that Clinton was seeking.
However, the letter would not include specifics of other tax cuts, such as for capital gains and estate, which will be left up to the congressional tax-writing committees, Lott said.
"I have said emphatically from the beginning, we are not going to write the tax bill in any kind of side agreement," Lott said.

The ranking Democrat on the House Budget Committee, John Spratt of South Carolina, told Democrats he felt they achieved 60 to 65 percent of what they wanted in negotiations and he intended to support the budget framework.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota had said earlier this week he believed Democrats would support the budget resolution. House Democratic Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri had said he would reserve judgment until he had time to review all the details.
